words.The post:
Nobody stays late on the last Friday anymore.

That's what Northwind's controller told me. Not "we saved six days." Not "the reports are cleaner." That.

When they came to us, their close took nine days. Nine. Most of it was the same ten spreadsheets, copied by hand, every month.

We connected their bank feeds and let the reconciliation run overnight. Last month they closed in three days.

The speed is good. But the part nobody puts in a business case is this: a shorter close gives people their evenings back. Month-end stops being something the team braces for.

If your close still runs on copied spreadsheets, read how Northwind did it.

#Accounting #MonthEndClose #Finance

words.The post:
Most closes run slow because of copying, not accounting.

Think about where the days actually go. Totals pasted from one spreadsheet into another. Invoice numbers re-keyed. Bank lines moved by hand into the reconciliation file.

That's not finance work. That's transcription.

Northwind cut its month-end close from 9 days to 3. The accounting didn't change. The copying did. Ledgerly moves the data, so the team spends close week closing.

If your close runs long, count the copy-paste steps before you question the accountants.

Read how they did it: [link]

#MonthEndClose #FinanceLeadership #Accounting

It's not the close that's painful. It's copying the same ten spreadsheets by hand, month after month after month.

On this episode of the Ledgerly podcast, we get into why month-end feels like Groundhog Day for so many finance teams, and why the problem usually isn't the people doing the work.

When the same numbers get retyped into ten different files, errors don't just sneak in. They multiply. The teams with calmer closes didn't get faster at copying. They stopped doing it.
